creator: Sabine Hossenfelder
title: Dark Matter Finally Detected?
full_text:
An experiment to see what might be the
first ever evidence for dark matter
particle. It's a single data point, so
we can't conclude much from it, but if
there was a real discovery, then this is
how it had start. So, I think we should
take this seriously and look at what we
knew and what it could mean. The data,
or maybe I should more accurately say
the datum, comes from the LUX Zeppelin
experiment. That's a very sensitive
detector in South Dakota in an old gold
mine about 1 and 1/2 km underground. And
in some sense, they still dig for gold,
the gold of the Nobel Prize, because
let's be clear, if we finally pin down
what dark matter is made of, that would
win a Nobel Prize for sure. It would end
half a century of stagnation in the
foundations of physics. This experiment
uses about 10 tons of liquid xenon at
minus 99° C. That's very closely
monitored for anything that bumps into
the atoms. It's so deep underground to
avoid cosmic rays and it's heavily
shielded to avoid contamination from
radioactive decays and so on. The idea
is that dark matter just goes through
all the rock and shields and on occasion
leaves a trace in the xenon. Now, this
one data point here is outside of the
normal background that they expect. If
it's really dark matter particle, they
calculate it would be a quite heavy one
with a mass of at least 400 GeV. That's
more than three times as heavy as the
Higgs boson, and that explains why the
Large Hadron Collider hasn't found it.
The energy simply wasn't high enough.
Indeed, the LUX Zeppelin collaboration
itself missed the event in an earlier
data analysis because the energy is so
high, they didn't look for it. The
statistical significance is between 2.6
and 3.4 sigma, depending on how you do
the analysis. So, that's vaguely between
1 in 200 and 1 in 1,000 chance to be a
statistical fluke. That's mediocre for
particle physics, but in cosmology, it
would be breaking news. And I have to
admit, it does look like an unusual
event. There are standard physics events
which can look like this, but they're
contrived. For example, you can have a
radioactive decay that produces a gamma
ray. The gamma ray happens to hit two
nuclei whose signals overlap, but the
second signal is so close to the wall of
the detector that it looks like both
came from the same nucleus. Possible,
but unlikely. Or an electron can be
spontaneously absorbed by a nucleus
which then spits it back out. The energy
would kind of fit the observation, but
the distribution,
possible but very unlikely. So, it's
difficult to explain. And there are
indeed some new particles which have
previously been proposed that are
compatible with this detection. There
is, for example, a pseudo Dirac
Higgsino, that's a type of
supersymmetric particle, or electroweak
multiplets. What particle physicists
have invented so many particles at this
point, it'd be surprising if there was
not at least one that fits. I give this
a seven out of 10 on the meter.
It's fine for what the data collection
and analysis and interpretation is
concerned. It does indeed look like an
odd event, and it could indeed be a dark
matter particle, and it's in a range
where that had not have been ruled out
by other data already. I don't see any
obvious red flags. My major problem is
one that these analyses don't account
for. It's that I think once you compare
the plausibility of some unlikely
standard physics explanation, like these
specific radioactive decay signatures,
to the plausibility of the dark matter
models, that's the question, what's your
prior? Shouldn't we take into account
that physicists have made all these
wrong predictions in the past, none of
which came true? You see, the LUX
Zeppelin experiment is an upgrade of an
earlier experiment that's run since
2012. This is a common story with dark
matter searches. They look for a
particle, they don't find it, they say
they need a more sensitive detector,
they upgrade it, they don't find it,
they say they need a more sensitive
detector, and so on. The
experimentalists justify their
experiments by saying the theorists have
theories for it, and the theorists
justify their theories with saying
there's experiments that could test
them. The experiments never confirm the
theories, but no one dares to question
this insanity because, hey, you never
know what they might find, right? Of
course, I'm not the only one who's
noticed this. The astrophysicist Stacy
McGaugh has commented recently, "These
experiments have run their course.
They've succeeded in failing. At what
point do we admit that and stop throwing
good money after bad?" Okay, but just
because Sabina thinks something's going
systematically wrong doesn't mean this
isn't dark matter. So, the brief summary
is obviously, we need more data. But,
yes, this could be the breakthrough
we've all been hoping for, and I grant
you permission to be the case,
we need a bigger detector. I find it
fascinating how much research goes into
everyday objects like the razors from
today's sponsor, Henson. This might come
as somewhat of a surprise to you, but
Henson's team have a background in
aerospace engineering. They've built
parts for the ISS and the ExoMars rover.
They use the same precision to design
their razor. They figured out at exactly
which angle the blades need to be
positioned so as to cut off hairs
perfectly and not cut your skin. The
pieces that hold the blades are not
plastic, but cut out from metal to a
precision of a hundredth of a
millimeter. I prefer my husband cleanly
shaven and without cuts. And Henson's is
by far the best razor I've seen at work.
Also works for women. And of course, I
have a special offer. If you buy a
Henson razor through my link or use my
code, you'll get 100 blades for free
along with it.
You've never shaved that side
effectively. Thanks for watching. See
you tomorrow.

notes.note: The LHC collides protons at 13-14 TeV, far higher than a ~375 GeV particle (3x Higgs mass), so collision energy isn't the limit. CERN researchers attribute non-discovery of heavier Higgs-like bosons to weak couplings and low production rates, not insufficient energy.
notes.claim: The Large Hadron Collider did not have sufficient energy to produce a particle with a mass of at least 400 GeV as a dark matter candidate.
notes.context_quote: that explains why the Large Hadron Collider hasn't found it. The energy simply wasn't high enough.
notes.context_paragraph: That's more than three times as heavy as the Higgs boson, and that explains why the Large Hadron Collider hasn't found it. The energy simply wasn't high enough.

sources.quote: The answer might be that the new boson behaves differently from the Higgs boson we already discovered. It might interact differently with quarks, or leptons, or both. Maybe it cannot be easily produced during the proton-proton collisions at the LHC. To summarize, its production could be suppressed.
sources.explanation: Confirms that non-discovery is attributed to low production rates and suppressed interactions (couplings), not a lack of collider energy.

sources.quote: a third undiscovered Higgs boson which is very heavy - with a mass in a range between three times and twenty times heavier than the Higgs boson we know.
sources.explanation: Confirms the LHC is already searching for particles in the specific mass range mentioned (3x Higgs mass).
Confirms the LHC's collision energy (13 TeV) which is significantly higher than the 375 GeV (0.375 TeV) mass of the particle in question.

notes.opus_reason: She says this in her own voice and without hedging: the candidate would weigh at least 400 GeV, "and that explains why the Large Hadron Collider hasn't found it. The energy simply wasn't high enough." Taken literally that is wrong, and the error is large. The LHC collides protons at 13.6 TeV, about thirty-four times the mass in question, and it has already excluded strongly produced particles well above one TeV, so a viewer who takes her sentence at face value comes away with a badly wrong picture of what the machine can reach. The real reason a 400 GeV higgsino or electroweak multiplet survives is that it is produced through the weak interaction only, so it is made far too rarely and its decay products are too soft to see. Published reach for higgsinos sits around 130 to 225 GeV and the papers give small production cross sections and large backgrounds as the cause. My hesitation is twofold. First, she has a defensible reading in which "energy" is shorthand for the collider's reach, since the rate for making heavy pairs falls steeply with the collider energy and the field's own answer to covering these particles is to build a higher-energy machine, so a flat "collision energy isn't the limit" is stronger than the physics supports. Second, the note's only source is a CMS page about extra heavy Higgs bosons, which is a different particle with different couplings, so the evidence offered does not actually cover the candidates she named. As a physicist and a well-known critic of this field she is likely to read the note as quibbling with a simplification she made for a lay audience.
